claims.text: Pulumi maintains a documented provider support policy that specifies how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
Some Pulumi providers receive long-term security updates while others do not.
Pulumi's provider support policy documentation is located at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
Pulumi does not automatically rollback changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs.
When an error or failure occurs during an update, Pulumi completes any pending operations currently in progress and then exits and reports the error or failure.

To accomplish a manual rollback after a failed deployment, you can revert the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and run `pulumi up` to update your infrastructure to its previous state.
Pulumi does not automatically query your cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`.
Pulumi compares the desired state declared in your program against the last recorded state to determine what changes to make.
Refreshing state requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack.
This round-trip requirement for refreshing adds significant latency, especially for large stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of your cloud resources.
You can refresh and apply your desired state in a single step using `pulumi up --refresh`.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The 'Refreshing state' page at /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/#refreshing-state exists and provides a detailed explanation of refresh behavior.
Pulumi resources have both a logical name and a physical name that differ from each other.
The logical name is how a resource is known to Pulumi and is part of the auto-assigned resource URN.
The physical name is how a resource is known to the cloud provider.
A resource's logical name only needs to be unique within a stack.
A resource's physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope, sometimes even globally.
Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a randomly-generated suffix appended afterward.
This auto-naming approach allows Pulumi to replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
With auto-naming, a resource's physical name will typically look like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket`.
You can disable auto-naming on a per-resource basis.
Disabling auto-naming lets you have precise physical names without random suffixes, but you lose the reduced-downtime replacement benefit and the conflict-avoidance benefit.
The auto-naming documentation page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/#autonaming.
You can use project or stack configuration to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The 'Auto-naming Configuration' page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/#autonaming-configuration.
Pulumi provides primitives so that secrets are stored in a secure manner in the CLI, state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
During an update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
You may pass `--secret` to `pulumi config set` when setting a configuration value, which causes the value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key that it uses to encrypt secrets for that stack.
Pulumi Cloud's per-stack encryption key is configurable to use your own custom secrets provider.

Because a different encryption key is used for each stack, encrypting the same value across two different stacks leads to different encrypted strings being stored in the respective `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files.
You cannot copy an encrypted secret value from one `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` file to another using a text editor.
To move an encrypted secret value between stack config files, you must use `pulumi config set`.
When you run a preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret configuration data.
Decrypted secret data is plain text during the execution of a deployment, and any part of the Pulumi program may access it using the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas in order to know what resources and parameters are available, and to determine the return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define your end state.
In Pulumi, the programming language is used for authoring your program and is not used for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages with programming languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol.
Because Pulumi programs support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, you rarely need to leave your IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, requiring explicit enabling via a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When an experimental Pulumi feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi providers receive no patches at all.
You can find the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi in the Pulumi Registry at /registry/.
When a major provider version is released, that is a signal to begin planning a provider version update.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources, and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, as well as performance improvements and bug fixes, without introducing breaking changes.
The recommendation is to update to the latest minor version on the current major provider version at least quarterly, and to minimally review provider release notes.
Patch versions of Pulumi providers are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.
The tilde operator in npm, for example ~1.2.3, can be used to always allow patch updates on the current minor version.
Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version.
Migration logic included in Pulumi provider major versions does not always work across multiple major versions.
Being two or more major versions behind on a Pulumi provider can accumulate a significant number of changes and may require a multi-step upgrade.
The 'Provider support policy' page exists at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
The 'Pulumi ESC FAQ' page exists at /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/.
The 'Pulumi Cloud FAQ' page exists at /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/.
The 'Pulumi Policies FAQ' page exists at /docs/support/faq/policies/.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version only until the next major version is released, if that comes before the 12-month window ends.

Pulumi's current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions includes AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.
The Pulumi Registry page for the AWS provider is located at /registry/packages/aws/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Azure Classic provider is located at /registry/packages/azure/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Azure Native provider is located at /registry/packages/azure-native/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Azure AD provider is located at /registry/packages/azuread/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Command provider is located at /registry/packages/command/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Docker Build provider is located at /registry/packages/docker-build/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the GCP provider is located at /registry/packages/gcp/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Kubernetes provider is located at /registry/packages/kubernetes/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the TLS provider is located at /registry/packages/tls/.
The Pulumi Registry page for the Vault provider is located at /registry/packages/vault/.
An LTS release on Pulumi's long-term support branch includes fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
An LTS release on Pulumi's long-term support branch includes fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship CVE security patches.
A Pulumi LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions.
A Pulumi LTS release does not contain new resources or new resource properties.
A Pulumi LTS release does not contain performance improvements.
A Pulumi LTS release does not contain non-security bug fixes.
A Pulumi LTS release does not contain compatibility updates for newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi providers will be compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at unless otherwise prompted via security fixes.
Exactly one long-term support major version exists per provider at any time under Pulumi's provider support policy.
When major version N+1 of a Pulumi provider ships, N+1 becomes the new current major (N) and the old N becomes the new long-term support major.

When a Pulumi provider's long-term support major version changes, the old long-term support major reaches end of life on the same day the new major ships, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within a Pulumi provider's long-term support major version, only the latest minor version receives patches, and earlier minors are frozen.
Pulumi LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Pulumi recommends that customers pin to a specific major version.
Customers pinning a Pulumi provider to a specific major version will automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version.
Older major versions of a covered Pulumi provider (older than the LTS major) receive no patches.
The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions until N+1 ships.

The long-term support major version (N−1) of a Pulumi provider receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, whichever comes first.
Provider major versions at end of life (N−2 and older) are not supported and will not receive updates.
Pulumi publishes a 'Best practices for maintaining provider versions' resource at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions.
The Pulumi Registry is located at /registry/.
Pulumi's 'Getting support' page is located at /docs/support/getting-support/.
